title: Acute Loin-to-Groin Pain - Renal Colic
patient_instructions: You are a 35-year-old man with sudden severe abdominal pain that began a couple of hours ago. It started on the right side of your abdomen and has now moved down towards your groin and lower tummy. If asked: it is sharp and severe, about 8-9/10, and comes in waves - you get intense pain, then it eases, then returns. Nothing makes it better or worse; painkillers have not helped much (the examiner may tell the candidate the pain has already settled somewhat). You feel restless and cannot get comfortable. You are passing urine more often and have noticed blood in your urine. You have NO fever, chills or rigors, no burning on passing urine, no vomiting (maybe mild nausea), no diarrhoea/constipation, no jaundice, no yellow eyes or dark stools. You have no previous kidney stones but a distant relative had them. You have had occasional right-sided cramps after fatty meals in the past. No previous surgery, no trauma, no groin lump. Ideas: you think something is seriously wrong. Concerns: the pain is unbearable and you are frightened. Expectations: you want to know what is causing it. Affect: distressed, writhing, but able to answer questions between waves.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor in the Emergency Department. A 35-year-old man presents with acute right-sided abdominal pain radiating to the groin. He is haemodynamically stable and his pain has partially settled, so you are NOT required to prescribe analgesia. Task: take a focused history, state the examination findings you would seek (you may request the PEFE from the examiner), reach a provisional diagnosis with your reasoning, and outline your differentials and initial investigations.
examiner_instructions: Reward a structured SIQORAA pain history, a systematic differential screen (GI, KUB, hepatobiliary, hernia, genital), and the request to examine including vital signs (do NOT let the candidate forget TEMPERATURE), abdominal palpation, renal-angle tenderness and urine dipstick. On request, provide: afebrile, renal-angle tenderness present, dipstick shows blood but NO nitrites/leucocytes. The provisional diagnosis is ureteric (renal) colic; strong candidates cite the triad of loin-to-groin pain plus microscopic haematuria. Critical safety points: (1) fever plus colic = obstructed infected system (urosepsis) needing urgent decompression; (2) in any patient over 50 with first loin-to-groin pain, actively exclude a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm; (3) consider testicular torsion in a male and ask to examine the genitalia. Confirm the candidate names non-contrast CT KUB as definitive imaging. Prompt if needed: 'What must you not miss in an older patient with this presentation?'

criteria: Introduces self, checks haemodynamic stability and asks about fever/temperature early
Structured SIQORAA pain history capturing colicky loin-to-groin migration
Screens KUB symptoms (dysuria, frequency, haematuria) and GI/hepatobiliary/hernia differentials
Requests focused examination including renal-angle tenderness and urine dipstick
States provisional diagnosis of ureteric/renal colic with the loin-to-groin + haematuria reasoning
Correctly interprets dipstick (blood positive, no nitrites/leucocytes, afebrile) to argue against pyelonephritis
Offers a structured differential list (pyelonephritis, appendicitis, biliary disease, hernia, testicular torsion, AAA)
Identifies fever + colic as an obstructed infected system requiring emergency decompression
Actively excludes leaking AAA in the over-50 patient and considers testicular torsion in males
Names appropriate investigations: MSU MCS, FBC, UEC/creatinine, calcium/urate, beta-hCG in women, non-contrast CT KUB
Empathic response to a patient in severe pain; clear lay explanation of the stone and why it causes pain
Provides safety-net advice including to call 000 if severe deterioration occurs

red_flags: Fever or rigors with colic - obstructed infected (pyonephrotic) system and urosepsis risk requiring emergency decompression
Leaking or ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm mimicking renal colic, especially in patients over 50 or with haemodynamic instability or absent haematuria
Testicular torsion presenting as loin-to-groin/abdominal pain in a male - surgical emergency with a ~6-hour window
Solitary or transplanted kidney, bilateral stones, anuria/urinary retention, or rising creatinine - all mandate urgent referral
australian_guidelines: eTG (Therapeutic Guidelines): first-line analgesia for renal colic is an NSAID (e.g. indomethacin or IV/oral NSAID), with opioids reserved for refractory pain; fever with colic mandates urgent assessment for an obstructed infected system.

RACS / EMST teaching: a first episode of loin-to-groin pain in a patient over 50 requires active exclusion of a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm before accepting renal colic - palpate for a pulsatile expansile mass.
Murtagh (Australian): non-contrast CT KUB is the gold-standard investigation for suspected urolithiasis; ultrasound KUB is first-line in pregnancy.
learning_objectives: Take a structured SIQORAA history for acute abdominal/flank pain and recognise the colicky loin-to-groin pattern of ureteric colic.
Interpret a urine dipstick to support ureteric colic and argue against pyelonephritis.
Construct a safe differential list that includes obstructed infected system, AAA and testicular torsion.
Select appropriate investigations including non-contrast CT KUB and understand pregnancy-specific imaging.
key_points: Murtagh's DxT: intense loin pain radiating to groin plus microscopic haematuria = ureteric colic; pain comes in waves lasting ~30 seconds with 1-2 minute respite and usually settles within 8 hours.
Haematuria is present in most but not all ureteric stones - a negative dipstick does not exclude a stone; CT KUB is definitive if suspicion is high.
Costovertebral-angle tenderness is not specific for pyelonephritis - it also occurs in ureteric colic and renal trauma.
Never forget the temperature - an obstructed infected system is a urological emergency.
In renal colic, first-line analgesia is an NSAID, not an opioid.

citations.claim: Ureteric colic causes intense colicky pain in waves, beginning in the loin and radiating to the groin, with the diagnostic triad of intense loin pain radiating to groin plus microscopic haematuria; maximum incidence 30-50 years, M > F.

The structured pain history used in this case (site, severity/intensity, quality/character, time course, aggravating and relieving factors, radiation, associated features) follows the standard AMC medical history structure.
Acute appendicitis is a valid differential for migrating right-sided abdominal pain that shifts and localises to the right iliac fossa within about 6 hours.
Urine testing is an essential, never-to-be-omitted part of the renal/genitourinary examination.
citations.source: Talley and O'Connor's Clinical Examination, 8th edition
